newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel court bars police over prisoner's "torture".
newsitem.headline: Israel court bars police over prisoner's "torture".

text.p: Israel's High Court on Monday ordered the Shin Bet secret police not to use "prohibited investigative measures" against a Palestinian prisoner said by his lawyer to have been under torture for the past month.

Israel's Itim news agency said the temporary retraining order would remain in effect until a hearing was held in two weeks on Ghaith Abdul Hafeeth Ghaith's petition against being tortured by his Israeli interrogators.
Ghaith, 25, from the West Bank village of Deir Ghassan near Ramallah, was arrested on July 13. He has not been charged, Ghaith's lawyer Alegra Pachko told Reuters.

"He's been forced to sit on a chair for the last month with a very thick sack on his head while the Israeli police play loud music to drive him crazy," Pachko said, adding Ghaith's hands and feet were swollen and discoloured from being tightly cuffed.
"He hasn't been able to sleep most of the time. They let him sleep occasionally for two hours, but he hardly can because his body aches from the pain," said Pachko.
"He has very bad headaches due to the hooding and violent shaking and keeps asking for a doctor, but they're not bringing a doctor."
Pachko denied Ghaith had any connection with militant groups.
"Yesterday, I submitted a petition to the High Court and today I got a temporary order...banning the torture until the hearing," the lawyer said.
Israeli and Arab human rights groups have long said a 1987 Israeli state commission's ruling that Israel's secret police could use "moderate physical pressure" sanctioned torture.
Israel in May lashed out at the U.N. Committee against Torture for calling on it to stop using "torture" in interrogation of Palestinian detainees.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's communications director David Bar-Illan said Israel was using methods that were employed worldwide against "terrorism" and that the committee's move "sentences to death future innocent victims of terrorism".
